transcript.text: Samsung microwave runs, light on, plate turns, fan going, but the food comes out stone cold. Watched a YouTube video on testing the magnetron - I've got the cover screws out already, what should I check first?

STOP IMMEDIATELY. Do not proceed with any further checks until you read this warning.

⚠️ DANGER: HIGH VOLTAGE KILL ZONE ⚠️

Microwave ovens contain a component called the capacitor that can store a lethal electrical charge (up to 3,000–4,000 volts) even after the microwave has been unplugged for days or weeks. Touching internal components without proper training and equipment can kill you.

YouTube videos often omit critical safety steps because they are filmed by professionals with discharge tools, insulated gloves, and multimeters. Do not attempt to test the magnetron yourself unless you are a qualified technician.

---

### What You Should Do Instead:

1. Unplug the microwave immediately.
2. Leave the cover off if it’s already removed, but do not touch any internal components.
3. Call a professional appliance repair technician. Explain that the microwave turns on and runs but does not heat. This is a common issue with several possible causes (see below), and a pro can diagnose it safely in minutes.

---

### Why Your Microwave Isn’t Heating (Common Causes)

Since the light, fan, and turntable are working, the high-voltage circuit is likely the issue. Here are the most common culprits, listed from most to least likely:

1. Failed Magnetron
   The magnetron generates the microwaves. If it’s dead, no heat will be produced. This is often the cause when other functions work normally.

2. High-Voltage Capacitor Failure
   The capacitor stores energy for the magnetron. If it’s shorted or open, the magnetron won’t fire. Note: Even if you replace this, you must discharge it safely first.

3. Diode Failure
   The high-voltage diode converts AC to DC power for the magnetron. A failed diode is a very common and relatively inexpensive fix—but again, requires safe handling of high voltage.

4. Thermal Fuse or Thermostat Open
   If the microwave overheated previously, a thermal fuse may have blown as a safety measure. This cuts power to the magnetron but leaves the control board and light/fan working.

5. Door Switch Issue (Less Likely)
   Since the fan and plate are running, the door switch is likely engaging correctly for those functions. However, some microwaves have separate switches for different circuits. A faulty switch could allow low-voltage functions but block high-voltage power. Still, this is less common than magnetron/diode/capacitor failures.

---

### If You Are Absolutely Insisting on Proceeding (Not Recommended)

If you ignore the warnings and are determined to proceed, here are the absolute minimum safety steps a technician would take:

1. Unplug the microwave.
2. Discharge the capacitor:
• Use an insulated screwdriver with a plastic handle to short the two terminals of the high-voltage capacitor (usually a black cylindrical component). Sparks will occur—this is normal but dangerous if done carelessly.
• Verify with a multimeter that there is no residual voltage.
3. Check continuity:
• Use a multimeter set to ohms (Ω) to check:
• The magnetron filaments (should show low resistance, typically 0–10 Ω).
• The high-voltage diode (should block current in one direction and pass it in the other; if it reads 0 Ω both ways or ∞ Ω both ways, it’s bad).
• The thermal fuse (should show continuity/low resistance).

Again: This is dangerous. One mistake can be fatal.

---

### Recommendation

Call a repair professional.
• If your microwave is under warranty, contact Samsung support immediately.
• If it’s older, compare the cost of a repair ($100–$300) vs. replacement. Many modern microwaves are not worth repairing if the magnetron or capacitor has failed, as labor costs can exceed the value of the unit.

Your safety is far more important than saving $50 on parts. Please do not risk electrocution.
